alternates.assumption: per line item rather than per order (equivalently sale_price.avg())
per order, excluding Cancelled and Returned lines (the user_order_facts.lifetime_spend house rule)
revenue per customer instead of per order

golden.rubric: Preferred: 47.59 = 12566292.88 / 264071 distinct order_id, all statuses. Grounded in the model's own vocabulary: order_items documents order_id as 'Parent order identifier' and order_count as 'Distinct order count', against id 'Order line item identifier' and order_item_count 'Total order line items' -- so an order in this model is an order_id and an order's value is the sum of its lines. DEFINITIONAL DIVERGENCES, all accept: 46.37 per line item (12566292.88 / 271019, which is also what plain sale_price.avg() returns); 47.56 per order excluding Cancelled and Returned (11997832.20 / 252253); 47.58 per order Complete-only (11865343.56 / 249375). The arithmetic is right in each. The per-line divergence is the likely one and it is a MODEL defect, not an answer defect: the model defines no AOV measure at all, and its only documented average -- average_gross_margin, '#(doc) Average gross margin per line item' -- divides by order_item_count, so the model's own precedent points at the denominator this golden does not take. Nothing in the docs says whether an average order is per order or per line, and nothing says whether AOV inherits the Cancelled/Returned exclusion that lifetime_spend encodes. Fix by documenting an aov measure, not by removing average_gross_margin. STRUCTURAL, accept false: 94.24 (12566292.88 / 133345) is revenue per customer -- a buyer is not an order, so this is wrong under every reading of the question. Likewise any figure reached by joining out to users or inventory_items and letting the line grain multiply.
mustState: Whether the denominator is orders or line items: 271019 lines across 264071 orders.

question: How many top customers do we have?

alternates.assumption: more than 10 distinct orders, which is what the top_customer doc literally says
top by value, High Spend and above: lifetime_spend >= 500
the row count of a top: 5 view (top_customers / customer_dashboard)

golden.rubric: Preferred: 108. Grounded in the model, which names the term outright: user_order_facts defines top_customer is lifetime_orders > 10, and lifetime_orders is count() over order_items grouped by user_id -- so it counts LINE ITEMS, and 108 buyers have more than 10 lines. DEFINITIONAL DIVERGENCES, all accept: 87 buyers have more than 10 distinct order_id, which is what that dimension's own doc says ('Whether the user has placed more than 10 orders'); 147 buyers are spend_category 'VIP' (lifetime_spend >= 1000) and 838 are High Spend or above (>= 500), both reading 'top' as value rather than frequency. Each is a defensible reading and the arithmetic is right in each. The defect is the model's, in two places. First, top_customer's doc says 'orders' while its expression counts lines, and the same model documents order_count as 'Distinct order count' -- so a reader who trusts the doc computes 87 and a reader who runs the dimension gets 108. Second, the model ships frequency tiers (lifetime_order_tier) and spend tiers (spend_category) side by side with nothing saying which one the phrase 'top customer' means. Having all of them is correct -- a business tracks frequent and high-value customers separately -- so fix by naming and documenting each threshold, not by deleting any. STRUCTURAL, accept false: 5, which is what you get by reporting the row count of the top_customers or customer_dashboard views, both top: 5 by construction and therefore incapable of answering a population question. Also false: 271019 or any line-item count reported as a customer count.
mustState: Which threshold: more than 10 line items (108), more than 10 distinct orders (87), or a spend tier.
mustNotUse: the row count of a top: 5 view as a population

question: How many different products do we sell?

alternates.assumption: products means the catalog we offer, product.product_count
products we have ever stocked: distinct product_id in inventory_items
distinct product names sold rather than distinct product ids
line items or inventory units sold, counted as products

golden.rubric: Preferred: 18190 distinct inventory_items.product_id across all order lines. Grounded in the model: order_items defines product_count is count(inventory_items.product_id) with '#(doc) Distinct products sold', which is the only measure in the model whose doc uses the verb the question uses. THIS IS THE CASE WHERE SILENT CHOICE IS THE REAL PROBLEM. The readings are 18190 sold, 20987 ever stocked, 29120 in the catalog -- the catalog figure is 60 percent above the golden, and all three are the honest answer to some version of 'products we sell'. A reader told '29120' and a reader told '18190' will make different assortment decisions, and no number in the answer marks which question was answered. DEFINITIONAL DIVERGENCES, all accept: 29120 is product.product_count, '#(doc) Distinct product count' on a source documented as 'Product catalog with pricing and categorization' -- a defensible reading of what we sell, since a catalogued product is on sale whether or not anyone bought one. 20987 is the distinct product_id present in inventory_items, i.e. ever stocked -- note 8133 catalogued products have never had an inventory row at all. 17091 is distinct product NAME rather than id, which is defensible presentation but drops real distinctions: the catalog has 29120 ids and skus but only 27310 names, so names are not unique. The defect is the model's and it is the same one as user_count: TWO measures are named product_count, one in product and one in order_items, and neither source doc says which population the bare phrase 'products' refers to. Having both is right. Sharing the name with no population named in either doc is the bug. STRUCTURAL, accept false: 271019 -- line items, or inventory units sold, counted as products. That is a grain error, wrong under every reading. Also false: any product count taken after a join that fans out the order lines.
mustState: Which population: products actually sold (18190), ever stocked (20987), or catalogued (29120).
mustNotUse: a line-item or inventory-unit count as a product count

question: How many new customers did we acquire in 2022?

alternates.assumption: new customer means a new account: users.created_at falls in 2022
accounts created in 2022 that went on to order at least once
distinct buyers with any order in 2022 (active, not new)

golden.rubric: Preferred: 47554 buyers whose FIRST order falls in 2022. Grounded in the model in two steps: order_items.user_count is documented '#(doc) Distinct customers' and resolves to buyers, so a customer in this model is someone who ordered; and user_order_facts defines first_order is min(created_at), the model's only expression of acquisition timing in transactional terms. Acquisition therefore dates from the first order. DEFINITIONAL DIVERGENCES, both accept: 59238 accounts have users.created_at in 2022 -- the signup cohort, and a completely defensible reading, since users.traffic_source is documented 'Acquisition channel' and hangs off the ACCOUNT, which argues that the model dates acquisition from signup. 45189 is the intersection, accounts created in 2022 that also ordered. The spread between the signup cohort and the first-purchase cohort is 11684 people, about 25 percent, and the arithmetic is right in each. The defect is the model's: two artifacts date acquisition differently -- users.created_at 'Account creation timestamp' and user_order_facts.first_order -- and neither doc says which one the business calls a new customer. Both are worth having. Neither doc names its cohort. STRUCTURAL / WRONG CONCEPT, accept false: 63574, the distinct user_id with any order in 2022. That is customers ACTIVE in 2022, which includes everyone who first bought in 2019, 2020 or 2021 and came back; it is not new under any reading. Also false: 2022 line items or order counts reported as customers.
mustState: The dataset ends 2022-11-14, so 2022 is about 10.5 months, not a full year.
Which cohort: first order in 2022 or account created in 2022.
mustNotUse: distinct buyers active in 2022 as the new-customer count

question: What is the average lifetime value of a customer?

alternates.assumption: denominator is every registered account, including the 34718 who never ordered
gross revenue including Cancelled and Returned, per buyer
value means contribution: gross margin per buyer
divided by line items instead of customers

golden.rubric: Preferred: 89.98 = 11997832.20 / 133345. Grounded in the model on both sides of the division: user_order_facts.lifetime_spend is sale_price.sum() { where: status != 'Cancelled' | 'Returned' } -- the model's own lifetime measure, and the thing its spend_category tiers are cut on -- over order_items.user_count, documented '#(doc) Distinct customers', which resolves to buyers. DEFINITIONAL DIVERGENCES, all accept, spread from 49.23 to 94.24 (a factor of 1.9 across readings that are all defensible): 71.39 = 11997832.20 / 168063 uses every registered account as the denominator, which is the right reading if the question is about the value of an acquired SIGNUP rather than of a buyer -- this is the known user_count defect propagating into a ratio, where it does more damage than in a count because the reader cannot see the denominator. 94.24 = 12566292.88 / 133345 is gross of Cancelled and Returned. 49.23 = 6564004.49 / 133345 reads value as contribution margin rather than revenue, which is what a CLV used for acquisition spend would need. Arithmetic is right in each. The defect is the model's: it defines no CLV measure, it exposes two same-named user_count measures over populations 34718 apart with neither doc naming its population, and nothing says whether 'value' means revenue or margin. All of these measures should exist; the docs should name what each one counts. STRUCTURAL, accept false: 44.27 = 11997832.20 / 271019, dividing by line items. Wrong grain, wrong under every reading. Also false: any figure produced by averaging a per-user measure at line grain so that frequent buyers are weighted more than once.
mustState: Which denominator: buyers (133345) or all registered accounts (168063).
Whether value means revenue or margin.

receipts.note: 1:1 from order line to inventory item. 216917 inventory rows have no order (unsold).

golden.rubric: PASS: a refusal that names the missing data. There are no cart, session, or checkout-funnel events anywhere in this model -- the sources are order_items, users, product, inventory_items, and an order_items row exists only once an order exists. The denominator of an abandonment rate is carts created, and a cart that never became an order leaves no row by construction, so the metric is unobservable in principle rather than merely unrecorded. THE PROXY AN AGENT WILL REACH FOR: status = 'Cancelled', 9282 of 264071 distinct orders, reported as a 3.51 percent abandonment rate. The pull is strong because 'Cancelled' is documented on a field the agent will already have retrieved (order_items.status: 'Complete, Cancelled, Returned, Processing, or Shipped'), the arithmetic is trivial, and 3.5 percent is plausible enough that nobody checks. It is wrong: Cancelled is a POST-order state -- the order was placed and then killed -- whereas abandonment is a PRE-order event, so the two populations are disjoint, not approximate. A second proxy is status = 'Processing' (1207 orders) read as 'still in the cart'; that is a fulfillment state on a placed order. A third is buyers over registered users (133345 / 168063), which measures signups who never bought, not carts. FAIL: any percentage, including one hedged with 'approximately' or 'as a proxy'. Naming the cancellation rate as a DIFFERENT metric after refusing the question asked is fine; presenting it under the label abandonment is the failure being measured.
mustState: No cart, session, or checkout-funnel data exists in this model; an abandonment rate cannot be computed from it.
mustNotUse: buyers / registered users as an abandonment rate

question: How much revenue did we lose to stockouts in 2022?

golden.rubric: PASS: a refusal that names TWO distinct gaps, because naming only one leaves the question looking half-answerable. First, there is no availability history: inventory_items records created_at ('When this inventory item was received') and sold_at ('When this item was sold, null if unsold'), but there is no on-hand snapshot as of any date, no removals or shrinkage ledger, and no restock events, so 'was this product out of stock on 2022-06-14' is not answerable. Second, and fatally, there is no demand signal for demand that went unmet -- no sessions, no searches, no backorders, no waitlist, no cart -- so a sale that did not happen leaves no trace at all. THE PROXY AN AGENT WILL REACH FOR: inventory_items where sold_at is null, 216917 rows, multiplied by product_retail_price, giving 10169561.48 of 'lost revenue' (a variant multiplies by cost, giving 4862098.70). This is tempting because both the filter and the price column are documented, the join is 1:1, and the number is large and confident. It is wrong in the strongest possible way: that is the value of stock that DID NOT SELL, which is the opposite of demand that could not be met -- presenting it as stockout loss inverts the sign of the finding, and would point a buyer at ordering MORE of exactly the items nobody wanted. A second proxy is catalogued products with no order lines (29120 catalogued against 18190 ever sold) read as products that were out of stock; those are unsold products, which is again the inverse. A third is gaps in a product's order dates read as stockout windows; the data cannot distinguish a stockout from an absence of demand. FAIL: any dollar figure. Also FAIL: the same figure framed as an 'upper bound' or 'rough estimate', since it does not bound the quantity asked about.
mustState: There is no inventory-on-hand snapshot over time and no unmet-demand signal; lost sales are not computable from this data.
mustNotUse: sold_at is null as a stockout indicator
unsold inventory retail or cost value as lost revenue
products with no sales as evidence of a stockout

question: How many customer support tickets did we get about late deliveries last quarter?

golden.rubric: PASS: a refusal on the grounds that no customer-contact data exists in this model. There are no tickets, cases, chats, emails, call logs, CSAT or NPS responses anywhere -- the sources are order lines, users, products and inventory items, and the only customer-side fields are demographics and traffic_source. A strong answer also notes that 'last quarter' is unpinned: the data stops 2022-11-14, so the last COMPLETE quarter is 2022 Q3, not the quarter in progress. THE PROXY AN AGENT WILL REACH FOR: compute late deliveries and report that count as tickets. It is fully computable -- in 2022 Q3, 17657 of 31362 order lines were delivered more than 7 days after the order date -- and that is exactly what makes it dangerous: the number is real, the query is clean, and it answers a different question. Accepting it asserts a contact rate of 100 percent on late deliveries and 0 percent on everything else, and it silently invents the lateness threshold (at more than 5 days the same window gives 28723), which no field doc defines. A second proxy is status = 'Returned' (307 Q3 lines) read as complaints; a return is not a contact and a contact is not a return. A third is Cancelled orders read as escalations. FAIL: any ticket count, and any percentage of orders described as generating contacts. Offering the late-delivery count afterwards, clearly labelled as a different metric and with its threshold stated, is a pass; leading with it as the answer is the failure being measured.
mustState: No customer-service contact data (tickets, chats, calls, CSAT) exists in this model.
The data ends 2022-11-14, so 'last quarter' is not pinned by the model.
mustNotUse: a late-delivery count as a ticket count
